neighborhoods.name: the Heights
neighborhoods.title: Heights
neighborhoods.blurb: The Houston Heights sits about four miles northwest of downtown, a grid of Victorian bungalows and craftsman homes threaded by the MKT Hike and Bike Trail and the White Oak Bayou greenway. Its commercial life runs along 19th Street's storefront row, the Heights Mercantile shops on Yale, and the restaurant strip down Studewood. The housing stock skews historic, with strict historic-district rules on renovation, and the business mix is small and independent: boutiques, studios, trades, and services run by owners who live nearby. Customers here actively prefer hiring local over calling a chain.

neighborhoods.name: Montrose
neighborhoods.title: Montrose
neighborhoods.blurb: Montrose sits barely two miles west of downtown Houston, one of the city's densest and most walkable districts. Lower Westheimer's curve carries its restaurants, vintage shops, and bars; the Menil Collection and Rothko Chapel anchor its museum blocks; and its side streets mix 1920s bungalows with new townhomes. Many of those bungalows now house businesses, and the neighborhood's customers are young, mobile-first, and quick to check reviews before spending. It is a place where a dated website reads as a dated business.

neighborhoods.name: Garden Oaks
neighborhoods.title: Garden Oaks
neighborhoods.blurb: Garden Oaks, with Oak Forest beside it, sits about seven miles northwest of downtown: ranch homes and cottages on unusually large, tree-heavy lots laid out in the 1930s and 40s. Its business spine is the North Shepherd corridor, where a wave of breweries, restaurants, and service businesses has replaced older industrial fronts. The homes are aging in exactly the way that keeps plumbers, electricians, and roofers busy, and the families in them tend to find those trades through neighborhood Facebook groups and Google rather than billboards.

neighborhoods.name: Spring Branch
neighborhoods.title: Spring Branch
neighborhoods.blurb: Spring Branch stretches along the Long Point Road and Hammerly corridors between I-10 and US-290, roughly twelve miles west-northwest of downtown. It is one of Houston's most commercially dense neighborhoods for small business: strip centers, light industrial yards, and one of the city's best independent food scenes, with deep Korean and Hispanic business communities. Housing runs from 1950s ranches under renovation to new three-story townhomes. Competition among trades here is thick, which makes the map pack and reviews the whole game.

neighborhoods.name: Katy
neighborhoods.title: Katy
neighborhoods.blurb: Katy sits about twenty-five miles west of downtown Houston along I-10, and most of its growth is master-planned: Cinco Ranch, Firethorne, and the neighborhoods feeding some of the region's most sought-after schools. Retail clusters at LaCenterra at Cinco Ranch and Katy Mills, and the housing stock is dominated by newer two-story family homes on HOA streets. New rooftops mean first-time service relationships: families here are choosing their plumber, dentist, and repair shop for the first time, and they choose from their phones.

neighborhoods.name: Cypress
neighborhoods.title: Cypress
neighborhoods.blurb: Cypress runs along the US-290 corridor about twenty-five miles northwest of downtown Houston, one of the fastest-growing suburban belts in Texas. Master-planned communities like Bridgeland and Towne Lake add thousands of new homes a year, the Cy-Fair school district anchors family life, and the Houston Premium Outlets and 290 frontage carry the retail. Nearly everything here is new construction, which means builder-warranty handoffs, first roofs reaching age, and households actively searching for the service businesses they will use for the next decade.
